title: The hypertrophy series: developing the values of size and strength
summary: NH separates the qualities of size and strength: size correlates mostly with volume and tonnage (mostly sets above six reps), strength with intensity and skill practice at low reps compensated by frequency. Bodybuilders still need strength in the program, outliers with great leverages must keep chasing size, and size develops more chronologically than numerically.
claims: To progress in size you'll have to progress in strength, but the focus differs
'Low reps for strength, high reps for hypertrophy' is false: low reps can be low intensity and high reps high intensity
Intensity correlates more with strength and volume more with size
Enhanced lifters can train only volume because anything works for them
Training for size, most of your rep ranges should be above six; below six you accumulate less tonnage
Strength is skill practice with heavy weights at low reps; powerlifting is singles and strongman rarely exceeds 15
Strength can be trained with few reps because frequency makes up for it
Bodybuilders shouldn't train the big three as often as powerlifters; powerlifters train the lifts, bodybuilders train movement patterns
Many fail to grow because they only know progression as adding weight to the bar, ignoring rep and set evolution
For a bodybuilder, strength and size both rise but one faster than the other; size can't rise while strength stays flat
Powerlifters who stall add volume to build muscle; bodybuilders must likewise keep strength as a factor in their program
Don't say 'I'm a bodybuilder, I don't train for strength'; strength promotes progression
Leverages and muscle insertions skew people toward strength or size; someone with great leverages may see strength skyrocket without much growth
Strength outliers who barely grow must not get discouraged and abandon training for size
Hypertrophy and strength share a wall but not the same room
Hypertrophy progression means lots of reps within a relevant intensity window and multiplying sets
Bodybuilders plan more chronologically (session length, time); powerlifters more numerically (weight on the bar)
Size is more time-dependent because of hormonal profile and slow tonnage accumulation; powerlifters can peak early and taper off
